operationalization: Fit seasonal increments of length or stature to a sine term whose amplitude declines as mean growth rate declines. A winter deficit that shrinks smoothly toward zero with age would support the damped-sine description; irregular seasonality, or an amplitude that does not damp, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: DATRAS
candidate_datasets.role: North Sea and nearby trawl surveys with length, age and haul date for plaice and haddock, used to estimate seasonal length-at-age increments

obstacles: Survey lengths are cross-sectional, so size-selective mortality is mixed with growth.
Open human series rarely repeat the same individuals at half-year intervals across adolescence.
Temperature, feeding and day length move together, so a pure annual sine is not isolated.
rationale: The fish half of the claim can be tested with open age-length surveys timed through the year, and damping is a sharp extra prediction beyond 'growth is seasonal'. Those surveys still do not follow individuals, and the human half still lacks a public longitudinal counterpart to Daffner's cadet table. The claim is therefore testable for North Sea plaice and haddock, and only weakly for humans.

operationalization: On Arizona ponderosa ring-width chronologies, compare a red-noise spectrum of the raw series and of 100-year smoothed means against a stable peak near 150 years over roughly 1390–1910, then repeat the test on an independent summer-drought reconstruction. A significant, stable 150-year peak would support the claim; a featureless continuum, or a peak that appears only after century smoothing, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: International Tree-Ring Data Bank
candidate_datasets.role: Ring-width measurements and site chronologies, including Arizona ponderosa pine, for a spectral test of a 150-year growth rhythm

candidate_datasets.name: North American Drought Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Gridded summer Palmer drought reconstructions from tree rings, used to ask whether Arizona moisture carries a century-scale oscillation

obstacles: A 500-year window contains only about three cycles, and 100-year smoothing can impose a smooth wave.
Ring width mixes moisture, temperature and stand dynamics.
The gridded drought product used here is densest after 1700, so the early part of Thompson's interval rests mainly on the ring measurements.
rationale: The stated evidence is ponderosa ring width, and those series are openly archived at far higher replication than the few trees Thompson smoothed. Standard spectral tests can accept or reject a stable 150-year line. Discriminating power stays moderate because century smoothing and red noise can imitate a long cycle, and because moisture rather than temperature was an inference from the regional climate rather than a separate measurement.

operationalization: Partition growth velocity into a water-uptake or turgor term and a metabolic term, using osmotic or pressure clamps at fixed metabolism. A large drop in elongation when turgor is lowered at constant metabolism would support the claim; unchanged velocity under those clamps would refute the claim that water uptake carries a large share of the rate.
obstacles: Turgor, water flux and metabolic rate are rarely published as a matched public table.
Plant-cell experiments are much denser than measurements on animal embryos.
Volume increase from water can be a consequence of wall yielding rather than an independent driver.
rationale: The Lockhart-style split between turgor and metabolism is a usable decision rule, but 'in great measure' still needs a chosen variance threshold. The relevant experiments exist for a few plant cells and early embryos and would have to be compiled from papers. They cover a small part of the stated scope, and water uptake is easily confounded with wall extensibility.

operationalization: Regress the abdomen-to-cephalothorax length ratio of Artemia on salinity, holding temperature and food as covariates and comparing populations raised across a salinity series. A positive slope, with named 'species' falling on successive parts of one curve, would support the claim; a flat or negative slope after those controls would refute it.
obstacles: Morphometrics sit in paper tables rather than one open archive.
Wild samples confound salinity with temperature, food and clonal lineage.
Thompson's own isotonic-versus-equal-density test is still not a standard column in those tables.
rationale: The ratio and the salinity axis are directly measurable, and several experimental and field studies already report both. There is no single downloadable morphometric database, so a test means compiling those tables, which cover multiple populations but not a balanced global design. Population identity and co-varying water chemistry remain serious alternative explanations of the same body proportions.

operationalization: Compare observed size-versus-age curves with the velocity curve of an autocatalytic reaction, asking whether growth shows an accelerating phase, a phase of falling acceleration, and a late phase of slowing or mass loss, and whether the late phase behaves like chemical equilibrium. Sharing those phases while the endpoint is differentiation rather than chemical equilibrium would support resemblance without identity; a growth curve lacking the accelerating phase, or an endpoint that is chemical equilibrium, would refute that qualified claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
candidate_datasets.role: Age trajectories of size for thousands of animals, used to compare growth-curve shape with an autocatalytic velocity curve

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards
candidate_datasets.role: Human length and weight references from birth through early childhood, for the early and middle phases of the growth curve

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Fish length-at-age series and fitted growth parameters, as rival functional forms beside an autocatalytic curve

obstacles: Logistic, Gompertz and von Bertalanffy curves share the same broad sigmoid shape.
Public trajectories often stop before the late loss of mass.
The claim already hedges resemblance against identity, so a moderate misfit is compatible with the wording.
rationale: Open growth trajectories are now abundant enough to score the three phases Thompson describes for many animals. The decision is soft, because he explicitly allows resemblance rather than identity and because several standard growth laws look alike through the middle of life. Terminal mass loss and the contrast with chemical equilibrium are much less well covered than the rising and slowing phases.

operationalization: Compare body size and body-proportion phenotypes of animals in which thyroid, pituitary or growth-hormone pathways are disrupted with matched controls. A change in both scale and proportions would confirm that such substances can alter form; size changes that are pure scaling, or no growth effect at all, would count against the claim as stated.

candidate_datasets.name: International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium
candidate_datasets.role: Knockout phenotypes for body weight, length and organ or skeletal measures, including endocrine-pathway genes

obstacles: The open screen is a mouse knockout panel, so tadpoles, birds and external doses such as iodine are outside it.
Some proportion shifts are secondary to illness rather than a specific growth stimulus.
rationale: The claim is existential: some internal and external substances accelerate growth and change proportions. Mouse endocrine-pathway knockouts, with open body-size and body-composition measures, are enough to confirm or fail that existence claim for internal secretions. External dosing and non-mammal examples remain scattered in papers, which limits scope but does not block a decision on the core assertion.

operationalization: The wording assigns natural selection a function, removal rather than origination. Fossil appearances and extinctions of large reptiles and mammals do not supply a variable that would count as origination-by-selection in one outcome and origination-by-growth in another.
obstacles: Stratigraphic appearance and disappearance are compatible with selection both producing and culling variants.
Growth-rate change and selection on growth-rate variants predict the same fossil shapes.
rationale: The sentence is a claim about the proper role of selection, not a statement with a distinct measurable consequence. Any pattern of exaggerated forms arising and later vanishing can be read either as Thompson reads it or as selection among growth variants. Existing fossil inventories therefore cannot settle it.

operationalization: After the early maximum, regress log regenerative velocity of tadpole tails on log time since amputation and test whether the slope is −2, equivalently whether velocity times time squared is constant. A slope near −2 would support the claim; a slope near −1, or an exponential decline that fits better, would refute it.
obstacles: Length-versus-time series are in individual papers, not a shared archive.
The first day or two after amputation is often unmeasured, which is where the maximum sits.
Thompson offered the square law for one tadpole series and only guessed it might be general.
rationale: The exponent is a clean quantitative target and distinguishes a rectangular hyperbola from neighbouring decline laws. Published tadpole-tail series, including the table Thompson analysed, contain the variables, but they have to be digitised and they do not cover regeneration at large. A small team could test the tadpole case; a general law of regenerative velocity cannot be scored from those series alone.

operationalization: Align regeneration curves and whole-organism growth curves on a common time origin at the start of growth, and compare the sequence latent period, rise to a velocity maximum, then slow decline. Matching sequence and comparable scaled shape would support the claim; a regeneration curve that stays monotonic, or a full growth curve that lacks the rising limb, would refute a shared shape.

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
candidate_datasets.role: Whole-organism size-at-age curves, the ordinary-growth side of a comparison with regeneration time series

obstacles: Regeneration lengths are scattered across papers and start after a latent period that is poorly sampled.
Many unrelated processes share a rise-and-fall velocity curve.
'Essential features' does not specify a numerical tolerance.
rationale: Ordinary growth curves are easy to obtain, and the qualitative shape Thompson names can be scored. Regeneration series are not in the same archives, and the early limb he treats as decisive is the part most often missing. Because the likeness is defined loosely, many discordant curves would still be called the same essential shape.

operationalization: After claw amputation, measure the regenerative growth rate of the stump and the growth rate of the intact claw, and predict reversal from whether the intact claw reaches the large-claw size class first. Reversal when and only when that ratio favours the intact claw would support the claim; reversal uncorrelated with the two rates would refute it.
obstacles: Paired rate measurements are spread across lobster, snapping-shrimp and crab papers.
Nerve supply, molt stage and a handedness program can reverse claws at the same sizes.
Form-follows-size has to be granted before the rate ratio is interpreted.
rationale: The decision variable is a ratio of two growth rates, which experiments have sometimes recorded. There is no compiled public series, and the taxonomic scope is several heterochelous groups studied separately. Even a compiled table would leave neural and molt-stage programs as serious alternative causes of the same reversal.

operationalization: Test whether fission in worm-like animals occurs at the wavelength predicted for breakup of a fluid cylinder of that diameter and viscosity, and whether fission tracks that geometry across unrelated groups rather than tracking clade. Agreement with the mechanical wavelength, including in close relatives of similar shape, would support the claim; fission at genetically fixed stations independent of tube dimensions would refute it.
obstacles: Fission position, body diameter and regeneration are not in one trait table.
Stereotyped fission planes in short flatworms already sit poorly with a pure fluid instability.
Regeneration after a cut is observable, but the 'tendency to segment' is not a separate measured force.
rationale: The claim combines a physical instability with ordinary regeneration and uses taxonomic distribution as evidence. Body form and fission mode can be compiled for a subset of annelids and flatworms, which is enough for a partial test. The mechanical wavelength is rarely measured, and developmental control of the fission plane is an alternative that existing descriptions often favour without a clean force measurement.

operationalization: At the age when growth velocity switches from rising to falling, measure surface stiffness or skin resistance and an estimate of internal driving force. A step up in resistance at that age, with driving force still high, would support the claim; a falling driving force at constant resistance would refute it.
obstacles: Growth curves are not paired with time-resolved tissue stiffness.
Histological differentiation coincides with many changes besides a firmer skin.
Internal growth force is not a standard archived variable.
rationale: The claim is a causal timing statement: the velocity peak is a sudden rise in superficial resistance rather than a drop in internal drive. Growth curves exist, and histology exists, but the paired mechanical variables do not, in an open archive or as a compilable series. Coincidence of skin differentiation with slower growth would not separate the two sides of the proposed conflict.

operationalization: In a shape space, compare the trajectory of an ontogenetic series with the trajectory connecting the same forms along a phylogeny. A shared path, within a stated tolerance, would support one road of transformation; ontogenies that bend away from the phylogenetic path would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D specimen scans from which ontogenetic and adult shape series can be measured for selected clades

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic backbone for ordering species-level shape differences

obstacles: Most scans are adults, so ontogenetic series have to be assembled clade by clade.
Shared allometry can make ontogeny and phylogeny look alike in a low-dimensional shape space.
Coverage is strong for a few vertebrate groups and weak for the stated scope of organic form.
rationale: Geometric morphometrics can test whether individual development and species differences follow the same shape path, and both scans and trees are public. Usable ontogenetic series are a minority of what is archived, so the test is a restricted-scope one. Even then, a straight path in a reduced shape space is only a partial discriminator from other growth rules that pass through similar intermediates.

operationalization: The sentence ranks the scientific value of descriptive cell anatomy relative to dynamical study. No dataset outcome would raise or lower that value judgment while preserving the wording.
obstacles: Value of a line of study is not a measured biological variable.
rationale: This is a methodological judgment about what kind of cytology is worth doing. Cell images and force measurements can be used for other claims in the chapter, but they do not confirm or refute a statement that structure has little value except inside a dynamical inquiry.

operationalization: Ask whether spindle and aster geometry persists when microtubule mechanics and motor traction are removed, and whether a magnetic-like body force is required to keep the figure. Collapse of the figure under mechanical disruption, with no need for a magnetic or electric body force, would refute the claim; a figure that survives loss of traction and tracks an applied polarised field would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Published mitotic image studies, including spindles under cytoskeletal perturbations

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Curated micrographs of spindles, asters and dividing cells

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Archived cell-division imaging studies for comparing mechanical and field interpretations of the spindle

obstacles: Reading 'polarised force' as microtubule polarity is a modern gloss on a magnetic or electric analogy.
Force-ablation measurements are sparser in repositories than the images of the figure.
Repository coverage is model cell types, not every animal and plant mitosis.
rationale: Images and perturbation screens can test the part of the claim that denies a mechanical explanation and requires a field force of the magnetic kind. That is a proxy for Thompson's analogy rather than a direct measurement of a magnetic body force, which lowers operationalizability. The mechanical account is discriminable where motors and microtubules are perturbed, and those experiments are public for a limited set of cells.

operationalization: Measure nuclear roundness against cytoplasmic stiffness or solidity across cell types, including muscle and secretory epithelia. Nuclei that are spherical in fluid cytoplasm and systematically deformed where the cytoplasm is stiffened would support the claim; spherical nuclei inside stiffened cytoplasm, or deformed nuclei in uniform fluid cytoplasm, would refute the pressure account.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Protein Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Subcellular images of nuclear shape across many human cell types

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Cell-image studies in which nuclear outline can be scored against cell type and cytoskeletal state

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Reference micrographs of resting nuclei in soft and structurally specialised cells

obstacles: Image archives rarely include a stiffness measurement for the same cell.
The nuclear lamina and chromatin packing deform nuclei without a change in cytoplasmic fluidity.
Roundness is compatible with an interfacial film and with a tense cortical shell.
rationale: Nuclear outline versus cell type is directly measurable in public images, and muscle versus soft-cell comparisons match the contrast Thompson draws. The immiscible-film mechanism is not in those images: lamina mechanics produce the same deformations. The shape correlation is therefore a partial test of the claim, strongest as a description and weaker as a force law.

operationalization: The claim identifies visible cell polarity with a polarised force distribution whose lines are the aligned particles. Molecular polarity, cytoskeletal tracks and a physical force field all satisfy that description, so no outcome separates the claim from its rivals.
obstacles: Aligned organelles are the observation the wording treats as the evidence of the forces.
Any successful polarity mechanism can be redescribed as dynamical polarity.
rationale: Morphological axes are easy to score, but the claim does not add a measurement that would be true of a force field and false of other polarity mechanisms. Particle chains are both the phenomenon and the supposed proof. The statement therefore has no discriminating empirical consequence.

operationalization: In living and unfixed cells, test whether the alveolar meshwork has foam geometry, including threefold junctions near 120 degrees, as expected for two immiscible fluids, and whether that meshwork is absent when fixation is avoided. Foam geometry in living cells would support the claim; a meshwork that appears only after coagulation, or a living network with filament geometry, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Live-cell and fixed-cell studies in which cytoplasmic network geometry can be measured

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Light and electron micrographs of cytoplasmic and nuclear texture for a foam-versus-filament comparison

obstacles: Historical fixatives are only partly matched by modern correlative datasets.
Cytoskeletal networks can mimic a mesh without being a two-fluid foam.
Interfacial tension of the supposed fluids is not in the image metadata.
rationale: Foam geometry is a quantitative signature, and public live versus fixed images can ask whether the reticulum is present in living cytoplasm. That tests the main factual content for well-imaged cell types. It does not directly show two fluids striving to separate, so a network that is real but cytoskeletal would refute the foam account only where junction angles and continuity are measured.

operationalization: Score fine cytoplasmic networks and granules in chemically fixed cells against the same cells or matched living cells, and separately score nucleus, vacuoles, centrosomes and spindle. Fine texture present in fixed cells and absent in living cells, with the larger organelles retained, would support the claim; the same fine texture in living cells would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Paired and matched live-cell and fixed-cell image studies of cytoplasmic texture

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Deposited light and electron microscopy studies spanning living cells and chemical fixation

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Reference images of organelles Thompson treats as real, beside fine cytoplasmic texture

obstacles: Not every historical fixative is represented by a correlative live-fixed pair.
Some granules are real and some are precipitates, so a single global fraction is an average over structures.
rationale: The claim names which structures should survive a live-versus-fixed comparison and which should not. Public correlative imaging already contains that comparison for standard cell types and common fixatives, and the analysis is a classification of structures rather than a new method. Coverage is incomplete for the whole history of histological technique, but it is sufficient to confirm or refute the claim that the fine texture is largely artefactual.

operationalization: Track chromatin position through prometaphase and test whether chromosomes move from the poles toward the equatorial plane as a diamagnetic body would, using magnetic susceptibility if the analogy is taken literally. Equatorial collection that disappears when microtubule attachment is removed, with no diamagnetic susceptibility of the required sign, would refute the physical reading; motion that follows an applied magnetic gradient as predicted would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Time-lapse mitosis studies from which chromosome position relative to the spindle poles can be tracked

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Still images of metaphase plates and chromosome arms for the geometric half of the claim

obstacles: Equatorial congress is also the prediction of microtubule attachment and congression.
Magnetic susceptibility of chromatin during mitosis is not an archived variable.
The wording is explicitly an analogy, 'after the fashion of' a diamagnetic body.
rationale: Public mitosis movies can confirm the kinematic half, collection toward the equator, for many cell types. They cannot show that chromatin is diamagnetic, and the rival mechanical account predicts the same positions. The claim is therefore only partly resolvable: the path is testable, the physical kind of force is not, without new susceptibility measurements.

operationalization: Align membrane or pole-to-pole potential of fertilised eggs with the cleavage cycle, and ask whether the animal-vegetal difference reverses at successive divisions and whether chromatin's electrical contrast peaks at mitosis. A large causal contribution, shown by division failing when those differences are clamped, would support the claim; potential fluctuations that are dispensable for division would refute a 'great part' in the process.
obstacles: 'A great part' has no numerical threshold.
Voltage traces aligned to cleavage exist for a few eggs and are not in one archive.
Potential changes can be consequences of membrane events rather than drivers of the division plane.
rationale: The concrete electrical patterns Thompson cites are measurable, and classic recordings for fish and amphibian eggs can be compiled. They cover few species, and correlation with cleavage does not show that the potential difference does causal work. Clamping experiments that would settle the causal share are sparse, so only a proxy test is available.

operationalization: During cytokinesis, decompose the force across the furrow into cortical surface tension and other contributions such as an actomyosin ring, and check that the division plane is the equator of the spindle. Division that proceeds when surface tension is held constant, driven by active contractility, would refute a necessary conflict with surface tension; a furrow that appears only when surface tension yields at that equator would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Time-lapse cytokinesis studies used as a geometric proxy for furrow position, not as a force measurement

obstacles: The claim says all cells, while force data exist for a handful of model types.
Cortical tension and active contractility are easily conflated.
Image repositories record shape much more often than tension.
rationale: Furrow position relative to the spindle is widely imaged and can be scored now. The force claim, a conflict with surface tension in every cell, depends on mechanical measurements that are scattered and taxonomically narrow. Active ring contractility is a rival that those limited experiments can sometimes separate from passive surface tension, so the test is informative only inside that subset.

operationalization: Measure egg cortical tension immediately before and after the first sperm enters, and record whether later sperm are excluded when tension is experimentally held flat. A prompt tension increase that is required for the block would support the claim; exclusion of later sperm by membrane potential or a fertilization envelope, with tension unchanged, would refute it.
obstacles: Tension time series at fertilization are in papers on a few model eggs.
The electrical fast block and the cortical-granule envelope are confounded with any tension change if they are not measured separately.
Species differ in which block acts first.
rationale: Failure of later sperm is not itself a tension measurement, but tension, membrane potential and envelope elevation have all been recorded often enough to compile a partial test. The rivals make different predictions, so the inference from polyspermy block to surface tension is decidable where those series exist. They do not yet cover animal eggs at large, and they are not in one archive.

operationalization: Track male and female pronuclei from sperm entry until they meet, and test three predictions: paths stay inside the triangle they form with the egg centre, curves are convex toward the line joining the pronuclei unless they start on a diameter, and they meet before the centre and only then move straight to it. That geometry would support the claim; straight paths, or a meeting at or beyond the centre, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Embryo time-lapse studies from which pronuclear positions can be tracked in model species

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Deposited fertilization and early-embryo movies for path geometry

obstacles: Ready-made coordinate tables are rarer than the movies.
Public movies are concentrated on nematode, mouse and echinoderm eggs rather than the frog geometry Thompson illustrated.
Meeting before the centre can arise from more than one force law.
rationale: The prediction is geometric and sharp, and fertilization movies in public archives contain the paths for several model eggs. Turning movies into a confirm-or-refute test still takes tracking, and the species mix only partly matches the eggs Thompson had in mind. The curvature and meeting-point criteria do discriminate this two-force picture from a straight mutual approach.

operationalization: The claim says mitotic figures follow from simple physical assumptions and therefore have only remote biological significance. A physical model that fits the figures would not measure significance, and a biologically important mitotic step can still be physically simple.
obstacles: Secondary biological significance is a judgment, not a variable.
Sufficiency of a physical model does not separate functional from incidental mitotic detail.
rationale: Whether a simple force picture can generate mitotic geometry is a modelling question already tied to other claims in the chapter. The further statement that those phenomena are biologically secondary does not name an observation that would be absent if mitosis were functionally important. Datasets of mitotic diversity cannot settle that wording.

operationalization: Using haploid counts for plant and animal species, compute the fraction with fewer than six chromosomes and the fraction with more than sixteen. The claim stands if both tails are small and the upper tail is the smaller; it falls if a large share of species lie outside 6–16, especially above 16.

candidate_datasets.name: Chromosome Counts Database
candidate_datasets.role: Plant chromosome counts, converted to haploid number where ploidy is known, for the frequency of counts outside 6–16

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Chromosome Count Database
candidate_datasets.role: Haploid and diploid counts across animal phyla for the same frequency test

obstacles: Plant records are often sporophytic diploid numbers, so haploid values need a ploidy assumption.
Animal sampling is uneven across phyla.
B chromosomes and sex chromosomes create within-species ranges.
rationale: The claim is a frequency statement about germ-nucleus chromosome number, and both plants and animals now have open count compilations large enough to estimate the two tails. The analysis is a histogram. Uneven taxonomy and diploid reporting reduce adequacy below a complete census, but they do not prevent a clear decision about whether counts are mostly confined to six through sixteen.

operationalization: Quantify mitotic characters, including presence of a visible spindle, chromosome number, chromosome form and arrangement, within species and between close relatives, and test their association with taxonomy. High within-species and within-genus scatter, and weak correlation with species identity, would support the claim; characters that diagnose species or close relatives would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Chromosome Counts Database
candidate_datasets.role: Within- and among-species plant chromosome counts, one of the mitotic details named in the claim

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Chromosome Count Database
candidate_datasets.role: Animal chromosome counts for comparing number variation with taxonomic distance

obstacles: Chromosome number is only one of the listed details; form, arrangement and spindle position are not in these databases.
'Not specifically related to the organism' can be read as several different association tests.
Number is often constant within species, which pulls against a blanket reading.
rationale: Open count databases can test the chromosome-number slice, including variation among relatives. The rest of the mitotic details Thompson lists, spindle position, chromosome shape and grouping, remain in the cytological literature and would have to be coded by hand. Species-constant chromosome numbers also mean the data can support the claim for some details and cut against it for others.

operationalization: Cross-tabulate early embryonic categories, yolk amount, cleavage geometry and chromosome number, against clades on a molecular phylogeny, and measure how much taxonomic structure those categories recover. Rare, scattered agreement would support the claim; categories that recover major clades at high frequency would refute 'seldom and accidentally'.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogeny independent of cleavage type and yolk class, used as the classification side of the comparison

candidate_datasets.name: Chromosome Counts Database
candidate_datasets.role: Chromosome-number categories to set against plant classification

obstacles: Cleavage mode and yolk class are not in a single open table and must be compiled.
Older classifications sometimes used the same embryological characters, so agreement can be partly by construction unless the tree is molecular.
The claim covers animals from segmentation onward, a wider span than any one compiled matrix.
rationale: A mutual-information test between early embryonic categories and an independent phylogeny is a direct reading of 'seldom and accidentally'. Trees and chromosome counts are public; cleavage and yolk still have to be assembled from monographs, so only a subset of taxa can be scored promptly. Using a molecular tree avoids the circularity of testing embryological groups against a classification built from those same groups.

operationalization: Relate the presence of visible cell boundaries in cleaving eggs to measured cortical tension, contrasting partial and total segmentation and unicellular versus multicellular organisation. Boundaries that appear only where tension succeeds, and disappear when tension is removed while adhesion is held fixed, would support the claim; boundaries set by adhesion or yolk distribution with tension unchanged would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Embryo image series showing whether cleavage furrows complete, a geometric proxy for individuality of cells

obstacles: Yolk amount and cell-cell adhesion predict partial versus total cleavage as well as tension does.
Tension during cleavage is not an archived field.
The phrase 'sphere of action of localised forces' adds no extra measurement.
rationale: Visible cell outlines are imaged in quantity, but the claim identifies surface tension as the force that creates them. That identification needs tension manipulations that are scattered and confounded with yolk and adhesion. Existing movies can test a proxy, completion of furrows, for a limited set of eggs, not the force ranking as stated for cells in general.

operationalization: Score whether cells that divide and live lack a visible centrosome, and whether centrosomes disappear and reappear, versus a requirement for a persistent material body. Cycles of disappearance, and division without a visible centrosome, would support the visibility clause; a universal persistent particle would refute it. The further claim that the centrosome is essentially a centre of force is not separated by those observations.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Cell-division image series in which centrosome presence, loss and reappearance can be scored

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Micrographs of animal and plant cells with and without visible centrosomes

obstacles: A body below the resolution of the image is compatible with both a hidden particle and a pure force centre.
Plant spindles without centrioles still have microtubule-organising material.
'Essentially a centre of force' does not specify a force to measure.
rationale: Public images can test the empirical clause that a visible centrosome is not always present and can come and go. They cannot test the metaphysical clause that the centrosome is a force centre rather than matter, because sub-resolution material and a force centre look the same in those images. The resolvable part is the visibility pattern, not the nature of the centre.

operationalization: Compare organismal shape in cases where cell number, cell size or cell form is altered, and ask whether the outline is unchanged. Shape that is invariant to cell number would support independence from the cellular partition; shape that scales with the cell grid would refute it. A continuous force field, as against cell-cell signalling, is not identified by that invariance.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D organismal form for the shape side of a comparison that still needs matched cell-number data

obstacles: Cell-number and cell-size series are not attached to most scans.
Signalling across cells can coordinate form without a continuous physical field.
The field is said to be unrestricted by protoplasmic continuity, which is not a column in morphological databases.
rationale: Independence of overall form from cell number is a testable fragment, and it has been studied in a few model organisms whose descriptions can be compiled. MorphoSource supplies shape, not the cell counts. The stronger wording, a continuous force field running through the whole organism, is not separated by those data from ordinary intercellular coordination.

operationalization: Compare the frequency of rounded versus plane contours in freely growing cells and organisms with the same frequencies in crystals and in cells grown under contact pressure. Dominance of rounded contours only in the free, fluid, imbibing cases would support the claim; abundant plane surfaces in free protoplasm, or rounded contours equally in crystals, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: BacDive
candidate_datasets.role: Bacterial cell-shape classes as a sample of minute free-living outlines

candidate_datasets.name: AlgaeBase
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic images of algae for scoring rounded versus plane contours

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Micrographs of cells and protoplasmic outlines grown with and without contact

obstacles: Shape databases record outline class, not whether growth was by imbibition.
Walls, shells and cortical tension also round a contour.
Pressure is rarely coded alongside the image.
rationale: A census of rounded versus plane outlines is feasible for bacteria, algae and imaged cells, which is a fair descriptive test of the predominance Thompson asserts. The mechanism, fluidity plus intussusception rather than surface deposition, is not in those records. Plane faces produced by pressure cannot be separated from plane faces produced by walls without additional annotation.

operationalization: For solitary cells and cells in contact, rank the contribution of surface tension against gravity, mechanical pressure and osmosis in predicting outline. Surface tension as the largest term across cell types would support the claim; pressure or cortical contractility dominating the shape residual would refute 'paramount'.
obstacles: 'Paramount' needs an agreed decomposition of shape variance.
Joint measurements of tension, pressure and osmosis are scattered and cover few cell types.
The wording already says 'probably', which softens a miss.
rationale: A force ranking is measurable in principle with aspiration, pressure and osmotic series, and such series exist for a small set of cell types in papers. They are not assembled, and they do not span solitary and aggregated cells at the stated scope. Shape archives alone cannot rank the forces, so the open data support only a proxy comparison.

operationalization: The claim equates organic symmetry with equilibrium under minimal energy and cites the amoeba as the case where both are missing. Symmetry is the evidence offered for equilibrium, so the association cannot be tested against a rival force law.
obstacles: Equilibrium is inferred from the symmetry it is then used to explain.
Asymmetric amoebae are compatible with many force laws, including ones far from a liquid film.
rationale: Symmetry of organisms and the irregular outline of amoebae are observable, but the claim uses symmetry as the mark of equilibrium and equilibrium as the cause of symmetry. No dataset outcome would favour that principle over other pattern-forming mechanisms that also yield symmetric bodies. The statement is therefore not empirically decidable.

operationalization: Measure rounding of protoplasmic drops and pseudopod tips when actomyosin contractility is inhibited and when interfacial tension is altered. Rounding that persists without contractility and follows interfacial tension would support the claim; rounding that requires active contractility would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Cell-rounding and perturbation-screen images used to see whether rounding survives loss of contractility

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Images of amoeboid cells and rounded protoplasmic blebs

obstacles: Modern cortical tension is itself often generated by actomyosin, so 'vital contractility' needs a stipulated inhibitor.
Tension values are in papers more often than in the image archives.
Pseudopod tips and bulk cytoplasmic drops may not obey the same balance.
rationale: Inhibition experiments can separate passive interfacial rounding from active contraction, and public image screens cover some of those perturbations. The decisive tension numbers are scattered, and the vocabulary of contractility has shifted since 1917, which makes the mapping only partly straightforward. For naked cells and blebs the test is informative; it is not yet a survey of protoplasm in general.

operationalization: For plasmodial movement toward damp, warm or nutritious sites and away from sugar or salt, measure local surface tension and test whether the tension gradient predicts direction as it does for an inanimate drop. Movement up the tension gradient predicted by each stimulus would support the claim; movement that persists when surface tension is uniform would refute it.
obstacles: Behavioural trajectories are common; simultaneous surface-tension maps are not.
Chemotaxis and thermotaxis signalling predict the same directions.
Sugar and salt change osmosis, viscosity and membrane state together.
rationale: Each taxis Thompson names has been recorded, so the behavioural parallel with inanimate drops can be illustrated. The account that local surface tension is the cause is not distinguished by those paths from sensory signalling. A discriminating test needs tension fields during the taxis, which remain unpublished as a usable series.

operationalization: Classify naked cells by activity state and by shape, and test whether active cells are amoeboid while resting or encysted cells are spherical. That association would support the descriptive claim; active spheres or resting amoeboid forms at high frequency would refute it. Unequal surface tension as the cause of the amoeboid phase needs a separate tension measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Micrographs of amoebae and other protists in locomotory and rounded states

obstacles: Activity and 'rest' are often inferred from the shape being explained.
Encystment adds a wall, so sphericity need not be a tension minimum.
Images are anecdotal relative to a survey of naked cells.
rationale: The activity-versus-shape association is a straightforward classification and can be attempted on published protist images. Those images are not a designed sample, and rest is sometimes defined by roundness, which weakens the test. The tension mechanism is an extra claim that the images do not carry.

operationalization: At the future bud site on a yeast cell, measure local surface tension through bud emergence and test whether a local drop precedes expansion, as against a polarity landmark that directs growth at constant tension. A tension drop that is necessary and sufficient for the bud would support the claim; budding at a marked site with no tension drop, or failure of budding when tension is locally reduced away from the landmark, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Saccharomyces Genome Database
candidate_datasets.role: Phenotypes of budding and cell-shape mutants, used to compare landmark-directed budding with a spontaneous tension drop

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Yeast imaging studies of bud-site selection and cell outline through the budding cycle

obstacles: Phenotype databases record shape and gene, not local tension.
Turgor-driven expansion and a tension drop make similar early bulges.
Coverage is excellent for Saccharomyces and thin for other budding yeasts.
rationale: Yeast budding is heavily imaged and genetically annotated, so the geometric sequence, local expansion then rounding, is testable now. The causal claim is a sudden local fall in surface tension, and the archived variables are genes and shapes rather than tension. Landmark mutants provide a serious rival, which makes the available test informative but one step removed from the force Thompson names.

operationalization: Fit each foraminiferal chamber outline to a surface of constant mean curvature and fit the whole test to the same class of surface. Chambers that match and whole tests that do not would support the geometric claim; chambers that fit no better than the whole shell, or that fit a non-equilibrium family better, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Endless Forams
candidate_datasets.role: Tens of thousands of planktonic foraminiferal images for fitting individual chambers against the whole test

obstacles: The images are two-dimensional views of three-dimensional chambers.
A constant-mean-curvature outline does not show that the chamber was fluid when it formed.
Desmids and many benthic chambered forms are outside this image set.
rationale: Endless Forams is large enough to fit chamber outlines of Globigerina-like tests and to ask whether the whole shell is a poorer minimal surface than its newest chamber. That is a real geometric test for planktonic foraminifera. It does not observe the fluid-then-solid sequence, and it omits desmids, so the mechanism and the full scope stay out of reach of this archive alone.

operationalization: Across a size series, measure how well outlines of whole organisms and of their cells match surface-tension surfaces, and test for a cutoff above which whole-body form departs from those surfaces while cell form still matches. That size split would support the claim; an equally good surface-tension fit for large body plans, or a poor fit already at bacterial and cellular scales, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: BacDive
candidate_datasets.role: Shapes and sizes of bacterial cells, the small-organism end of the comparison

candidate_datasets.name: AlgaeBase
candidate_datasets.role: Images of unicellular and small multicellular algae at intermediate sizes

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D forms of larger organisms, the end of the series where non-molecular forces should dominate

obstacles: Shape class is not a fit residual to a surface-tension surface.
Walls and skeletons change with size along with the surface-to-volume ratio.
The three archives do not share a common morphometric protocol.
rationale: Public records span bacteria, small algae and large animals, so a size-stratified fit to surface-tension forms is possible after harmonising outlines. The archives were not built for that fit, and other size-linked structures predict a similar cutoff. The result would be informative for a subset of taxa and still confounded as a demonstration that molecular surface forces are the cause.

operationalization: Classify outlines of unicells and cells in simple aggregates as plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid or nodoid, and test whether spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the most frequent, including during growth and division. That frequency ranking would support the claim; a ranking led by other families, or by irregular outlines, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: BacDive
candidate_datasets.role: Bacterial shape classes that approximate spheres and cylinders, without an unduloid code

candidate_datasets.name: AlgaeBase
candidate_datasets.role: Images of unicellular algae whose outlines can be assigned to Plateau's surfaces

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Cell micrographs for scoring surface type in simple aggregates

obstacles: Bacterial vocabularies collapse unduloids into rods or spirals.
Protist coverage in open shape tables is much thinner than bacterial coverage.
Transitions during growth need time series, which these archives mostly lack.
rationale: The six-way classification is well defined, and bacterial shape compilations already separate spheres and cylinders at large sample size. Unduloids and the protists where Thompson saw them are poorly coded, and developmental transitions are not in the tables. A frequency ranking is therefore available for a biased subset, not for unicells in general.

operationalization: On free end cells of Spirogyra and similar filaments, measure cylinder radius R and end-cap height, and test the predictions that cap height is about 0.27R and that the cap is a portion of a sphere of radius 2R subtending 60 degrees. A tight cluster around those values would support the claim; a mean far from 0.27R, or a cap radius other than 2R, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: AlgaeBase
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic images of Spirogyra and other filamentous algae from which end-cap proportions can be measured

obstacles: AlgaeBase images are illustrations, not a random sample of free end cells.
Turgor and wall thickness are not recorded with the photographs.
The numerical target assumes uniform wall tension, which may vary along the filament.
rationale: The cap proportions are a sharp geometric prediction and a poor fit would refute them. The raw material is public micrographs rather than a measurement table, so a test requires digitising ends, mainly of Spirogyra. That is feasible for a restricted scope and does not by itself show that uniform wall tension is the cause of whatever ratio is found.

operationalization: On viscid spider capture threads, measure coating radius, bead spacing and bead-size alternation, and compare spacing with the circumference instability threshold and the Rayleigh wavelength. Spacing a little longer than the inviscid prediction, with equal primary beads, would support the claim; a spacing unrelated to cylinder radius, or beads that do not form at that threshold, would refute it.
obstacles: Micrographs are concentrated on a few orb-weaver species and often illustrate rather than sample the thread.
The axial fibre and glue viscosity both shift the ideal wavelength.
No public morphometric table of bead spacing exists.
rationale: The instability criterion and the expected spacing are quantitative and distinguish this account from an arbitrary glue pattern. The measurements exist as published micrographs and would have to be compiled. They are too narrow taxonomically, and too entangled with viscosity and the core fibre, for a definitive test across orb-weavers, but they are enough for a partial one.

operationalization: Measure notch spacing on hydroid calycle rims and annulation spacing on their stems, and test whether both match the wavelength of a surface-tension instability on a fluid rim or cylinder of that radius. A shared match to that wavelength would support one surface-tension cause; spacings set by polyp size or genetic segmentation, independent of radius, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Digitized hydroid specimens, some imaged, from which calycle rims and stem annulations can be measured

obstacles: Specimen portals provide images and occurrences, not notch measurements.
Growth pulses and patterned perisarc secretion can mimic splash-like spacing.
The structures are fossilised as rigid perisarc, so the fluid stage is not observed.
rationale: Museum images make a geometric comparison of rim notches and stem rings possible for campanularian hydroids. That comparison is only a proxy for a shared surface-tension cause, because the same regularity can be produced by periodic growth. The fluid or semifluid stage Thompson invokes is not in the specimens, which are already solidified.

operationalization: Measure wall anisotropy, for example cellulose microfibril orientation, against axial versus radial extension in freely grown cylindrical cells, and compare isotropic-wall mutants or treatments. Cylinders where extension is easier along the axis, and a shift toward spheres when anisotropy is lost, would support the claim; cylinders with isotropic walls, or no shape change when anisotropy is removed, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: AlgaeBase
candidate_datasets.role: Images of Spirogyra and other free filaments for the cylindrical form, not for wall-polymer orientation

obstacles: Microfibril angle and growth anisotropy are published for model cells, not archived with the algal images.
External constraint is hard to rule out for cells inside a filament.
Turgor pressure is a necessary partner of wall anisotropy, so the wall is not the sole variable.
rationale: The prediction that an anisotropic wall yields a cylinder, and an isotropic wall a rounder cell, is a strong discriminator and has been measured in several plant and algal systems. Those paired measurements are in papers rather than a shape database, and AlgaeBase supplies only the outlines. The test is therefore available for a subset of free walled cells after compilation, not for elongated cells in general.

operationalization: Count distinct form classes among bacteria, protozoa and other minute cells, and test whether that count is small and shifts with physical conditions in the way surface-tension surfaces would. A short list of forms that tracks temperature, medium or osmotic state would support the claim; a wide form range at the same small sizes, uncorrelated with physical conditions, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: BacDive
candidate_datasets.role: Standardised bacterial and archaeal cell-shape records for estimating how many forms are actually used

candidate_datasets.name: AlgaeBase
candidate_datasets.role: Images and taxonomy of microscopic algae as a second sample of minute-cell outlines

obstacles: Shape fields are coarse categories, so 'limited' depends on the coding scheme.
A short list of forms can be phylogenetic conservatism rather than molecular-force control.
Protozoa are poorly represented next to bacteria.
rationale: Bacterial shape compilations are large enough to show that described forms fall into a few classes, which addresses the descriptive half of the claim for prokaryotes. The causal half, control by molecular forces, is not a field in those databases, and the same limited menu is predicted by shared ancestry. Algal images broaden the taxa slightly without supplying the force measurements.

operationalization: Ask how often cell shape class uniquely identifies a bacterial species, and how much shape of the same strain changes with growth phase, medium and preparation. Low identifiability together with large within-strain shape change would support the claim; shape that stably diagnoses species across conditions would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: BacDive
candidate_datasets.role: Strain-level cell shape, size and taxonomy for testing whether form identifies species

obstacles: Most strains carry one curated shape, not a series across life stages and preparations.
Shared rod or coccus shapes show low identifiability even when each species is morphologically stable.
Physiological specificity is a much larger character set than the shape field.
rationale: BacDive can test the identification half directly: many species share a shape class, so form seldom names the species. It does not systematically record plasticity across life stage, medium and preparation, which is the mechanism the claim gives for that failure. The open data therefore resolve a proxy, morphological non-specificity, and leave the plasticity statement only partly tested.

operationalization: Fit Vorticella bell outlines to the unduloid family between two unequal end rings, the stalk junction and the ciliary ring, and test whether species form a continuous series from near-cylinder to near-sphere. A good unduloid fit across that series would support the claim; systematic residuals, or a better fit to another surface family, would refute it.
obstacles: Bell outlines are in monographs and scattered photographs, not a morphometric archive.
Species sampling in illustrations favours distinctive bells.
A two-dimensional silhouette under-determines a surface of revolution.
rationale: An unduloid bounded by two rings is a specific curve family, so a fit to photographed bells can confirm or reject it for the species that have been drawn. There is no public coordinate dataset, and the taxonomic series would have to be built from plates. The mathematics is discriminating; the available images support only a partial, illustration-biased test.

operationalization: Fit loricas of Salpingoeca, Tintinnus and similar protozoa to the least-area surface available given their attachments, typically an unduloid, and ask whether form is fixed by that fit. A least-area match would support the geometric half. A protective purpose is not a separate measurable outcome, so it cannot be scored against the efficient-cause wording.
obstacles: Lorica outlines are scattered in taxonomic plates.
Protection is not an observable rival to set against a surface fit.
Adsorption into the surface film, as against secreted wall material, is not recorded with the outline.
rationale: The least-area geometry can be tested the same way as other unduloid claims, but only by compiling images, and only for a few loricate genera. The denial of a protective purpose does not change any predicted measurement: a well-fitting unduloid can still be protective. Adsorption as the route by which the pellicle forms is likewise missing from the morphological record, so existing data reach only the shape proxy.
